doc.title: Al Chez interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, February 13, 2019

title: Atlantic City Expressway with Jon Bon Jovi and meeting Mr. DeNicola
summary: At 15 Chez joined Jon Bon Jovi's band, playing the Fast Lane in Asbury Park, and met his high school band director who watched out for him.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: I don’t know what a banker lives like. I have no idea. I had a bunch of jobs when I was like my first couple of years in high school. I’ve been doing this a long time. So when I was like 15 I got a call to join — I’ve been very fortunate. I was 15 and I got a call to join a band starting in Sayreville. And the rehearsal, I knew a guy from the drum and bugle corps that went to Sayreville High School and he says this guy’s starting a band and he’s looking for a trumpet player, here’s the address, go talk to this guy. The guy’s last name was Bon Jovi. Bongiovi. And it was Jon Bon Jovi was the lead singer of this band, the Atlantic City Expressway that we started, he started. We were founding members. We were 15, 16 years old. Did a Battle of the Bands and lost to a country band. And then we started playing down at the Stone Pony and like the Fast Lane at Asbury Park. Some of the guys just got their license and we would have to go — we played every Wednesday night down at the Fast Lane which was around the corner from the Stone Pony in Asbury Park. The cool thing was we would get the head dressing room because we weren’t old enough to be in the club, never mind work in the club back then. We’re talking 1977, 1978. And the head dressing room had an alleyway by it. And if like the cops or the alcohol bureau would come into the club they would put this red light in and that would mean we would have to run into the alley because we weren’t allowed to be in the club. Okay? It was kind of a wild way to grow up but we would have to go — we would play Wednesday night, we would do that, and then I grew up in Edison, New Jersey which is about an hour and a half from Asbury Park, I’d have to get back home and I had school. You know? That was my first year of high school. I met my band director at one of those gigs. That was another one. We’re the headliner. It’s a Wednesday and there’s a band called Boulevard East. And they’re the warm-up band, older guys. And I’m sitting at the bar, okay? About 16 I guess. And the trumpet player from the other band comes up and he goes you sound great. And I was like thank you. He goes where do you live? You live down here? I said no, I live in Edison. He goes really. He goes where do you go to school? I go I go to J.P. Stevens High School. He’s like so what do you do, is this your
full time job? He goes no I’m a band director. I’m like that’s amazing where are you — ? He’s like I’m the band director at J.P. Stevens High School. And I was like, I’m at the bar.
And this is a coke I have.

Yeah. So I met my band director. He was amazingly great. And if it wasn’t for him you know I don’t know if I would have got through high school you know. Besides, I’m like a Hall of Fame member of my high school. I’m in the Hall of Honors and everything like that, because of guys like him. He knew what I was doing, you know. So the next day I hear, “Alan Chez please report to Mr. DeNicola’s office.” And I’m like oh I’m going to get in trouble. I was in there, I was drinking. He comes in and he says, “Alan” he’s got my transcript in front of him, and he goes, “did you make it to school on time today?” I said, “Yes I did, you could look.” He said, “What time did you get home?” I said, “I got home about quarter to four. Three forty-five I got home last night.” He goes, “And you made it to school?” I said, “Yes.” He says, “When do you have English?” I said, “I have English third period.” He goes, “You’re only getting a C in English, you’re going to have to pick that up.” I said, “Yeah.” And gym and everything. He says, “There’s a couch in my office” he goes, “go take a nap, I’ll wake you up for English.” So he took care of me. But if I started doing bad in a class, oh my God, he was worse than my dad. So he was a good guy. Thank you Mr. DiNicola. There you go. He’s still the band director there, and I run one of the marching bands at the high school that I went to, one of the marching bands, and he’s still the band director. He’s getting into the Band Master’s Hall of Fame. He just got put in there this year.
